question: In healthy adults aged 60-80, does overnight phase-locked closed-loop acoustic stimulation of slow oscillations, compared with sham, increase SO-spindle coupling and overnight offline gains on a finger-tapping motor sequence task, and does the size of the gain scale with the number of stimuli delivered?
why: The only closed-loop acoustic stimulation data with a motor outcome come from one afternoon-nap study in healthy (non-older) adults: stimulation raised coupled SO-spindle events, gave no group effect on memory, but showed a dose-response with stimulation rate (c0083-c0085). In older adults, the spindle-targeted interventions tried so far (spindle-tACS, TMR) did not improve motor consolidation, and TMR even lowered spindle density (c0022, c0027, c0029, c0052). Coupling is reported to be reduced with age (c0008). No study in this set applies whole-night CLAS to older adults with a procedural outcome.

question: In healthy adults aged 60+ with overnight PSG after motor sequence training, does SO-spindle coupling strength or phase predict sleep-dependent offline gains once fast-spindle density is entered in the same preregistered model?
why: The evidence conflicts. Coupling tracked offline gains in older adults after a nap on a cognitive procedural task (c0009) and in young nappers (c0086). In two overnight studies, including the largest (n=173), coupling did not predict consolidation while fast-spindle density did (c0089, c0109, c0108). Even the direction of the age effect on coupling disagrees: lower in older adults in one study (c0008), higher in another (c0090). No study has tested coupling and spindle density against each other, with consistent detection methods, in an older sample powered for that comparison.

question: In healthy adults aged 60-80 randomised to sleep vs wake retention intervals, do overtraining (extended practice to asymptote) and effector type (individuated-finger vs whole-hand sequence) interact to determine whether sleep-dependent motor sequence gains appear?
why: Older adults' failure to show sleep-dependent gains seems to depend on the task. A whole-hand version of the sequence task brought back overnight gains where the finger version did not, and this has been put down to declining fine dexterity (c0080-c0082, c0068). Overtraining restored sleep benefit in one sample (c0088) but not in two others (c0049, c0094). Each factor has been tested only alone, in small samples (n≈17-24), so it is unknown whether the effects add up or whether one masks the other.

question: In a young-vs-older adult comparison on the finger-tapping task, does the age difference in sleep-vs-wake offline gains survive when gain scores use the final-block (not averaged) measure, reactive inhibition is controlled with spaced training blocks, and time-of-testing is counterbalanced?
why: A meta-analysis (n=1296) found that the apparent sleep benefit for motor sequence learning disappears once averaging in gain scores, reactive inhibition, time of testing and training duration are accounted for. It also flagged elderly status as a moderator (c0038, c0039). The age-comparison experiments that report reduced sleep-dependent consolidation in older adults (c0031, c0034, c0054, c0087, c0107) do not use these artefact controls. So it is unclear whether the 'age deficit' is a real loss of sleep-dependent consolidation, or a difference in how young and old adults show reactive-inhibition recovery.

question: In adults aged 65+ with moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea, does 4-12 weeks of adherent CPAP, compared with sham CPAP, improve overnight motor sequence consolidation, and is improvement mediated by restored N2 spindle density or reduced sleep fragmentation?
why: OSA severity correlates with worse motor procedural learning in older adults (c0044). The only intervention tested is a single night of nocturnal oxygen, which reduced hypoxemia but did not change procedural learning (c0045, c0046). That leaves open whether fragmentation rather than hypoxemia is the active ingredient (c0004, c0074). No randomised trial in this corpus tests sustained CPAP against a procedural outcome in older adults.

question: In older adults (60+), does a post-training daytime nap of at least 60 minutes containing N2 spindles produce larger 24-h motor sequence retention than matched wake, and does the effect depend on explicit vs implicit sequence knowledge?
why: Nap studies in older adults split almost evenly. A nap helped explicit SRTT and motor sequence consolidation in some (c0013, c0040), and a systematic review concluded naps help motor learning (c0047). Other crossover and randomised studies with short and long naps found no effect in healthy older adults, Parkinson's disease or stroke (c0010, c0050, c0051, c0079). These studies differ in nap length, task explicitness and retest timing, and the largest has n=64, so the null results cannot be told apart from low power or design heterogeneity.

question: In chronic stroke survivors aged 60+, does a full night of sleep, compared with a daytime nap or an equivalent wake interval, produce offline gains on a paretic-hand motor sequence task, and do these gains predict functional upper-limb recovery over rehabilitation?
why: A review concluded that sleep improves motor performance after stroke compared with wake, while healthy older controls show no such benefit (c0066, c0067). A randomised nap study in chronic stroke found no sleep-dependent consolidation either after the nap or after a following night (c0078, c0079). It is unclear whether the benefit is limited to nocturnal sleep, to particular lesion profiles, or comes from comparisons with young controls. No study links the size of offline gains to rehabilitation outcomes.

question: Do older adults with amnestic mild cognitive impairment show reduced overnight sleep-dependent gains on a motor sequence task compared with cognitively normal age-matched controls, and is the difference explained by fast-spindle density or N3 slow-wave activity on PSG?
why: MCI is named as a population of interest, and SWS and spindle reductions are described across healthy ageing and MCI (c0001, c0002). Yet every procedural consolidation study here uses healthy older adults, Parkinson's disease, stroke, OSA or depression (c0010, c0044, c0078, c0103). Fast-spindle density is the most consistent microstructural predictor of motor consolidation in older samples (c0035, c0108). No claim tests whether that pathway is further impaired, or relatively spared, in MCI, where procedural memory is often thought preserved.

question: In older adults, does fronto-central white matter integrity (corona radiata, corpus callosum on DTI) and motor-network grey matter volume moderate the motor consolidation benefit of a spindle- or slow-wave-targeting intervention (TMR, CLAS), so that only people with preserved structure respond?
why: Structural MRI explains a lot of the age-related loss in sleep oscillations: white matter integrity predicts frontal fast-spindle loss and moderates whether spindles support overnight motor consolidation (c0036, c0037). Grey matter loss in motor cortex and striatum mediates reduced nap delta (c0092). Sufficient motor-network activation appears necessary for sleep-facilitated consolidation (c0015). Recent older-adult TMR and tACS trials were null on average (c0022, c0027, c0052) but did not stratify by structure. Neuroimaging combined with closed-loop sleep manipulation now makes it testable whether the null results hide structure-dependent responders.

question: In healthy adults aged 60+, does evening training (sleep within ~2 h) vs morning training (with a matched 24-h retest) increase motor sequence retention at 24 h and 1 week, on both a finger-tapping task and a gross-motor sequence task?
why: One study in elderly participants found that evening finger-tapping training produced extra overnight and 1-week gains compared with morning training (c0033). The largest age-comparison study (n=173, gross-motor sequence, ambulatory PSG) found training time had no effect on consolidation (c0111). The meta-analysis lists time of testing as a strong moderator (c0038, c0039). The disagreement could come from task (fine vs gross motor) or from the delay before sleep. That needs a direct factorial test in older adults, because training timing is a cheap and practical rehabilitation lever.

question: In older adults learning a gross-motor ballistic skill (e.g., dart throwing), does overnight sleep reduce 24-h retention compared with an equal daytime wake interval, and is any loss associated with N3 slow-wave activity rather than spindles?
why: One study (n=60 older adults) reported that nocturnal sleep harmed dart-throwing retention in older adults, the only claim of a negative sleep effect on motor memory (c0096). In contrast, whole-hand and gross-motor sequence tasks restored or showed sleep-related gains (c0081, c0107). A separate nap study found that entering SWS was linked to worse visuomotor maze performance (c0114). A harmful effect of sleep has not been replicated, and the sleep stage behind it has not been measured with PSG.

question: In healthy adults aged 60-85, does pharmacological REM suppression (e.g., a single SSRI/SNRI dose) after motor sequence or mirror-tracing training, compared with placebo, reduce overnight procedural gains, while N2 spindle density is held constant?
why: Reviews assign procedural consolidation to REM sleep and say REM-related procedural consolidation is impaired in older adults (c0005, c0058). The only direct evidence in older people is a 2003 correlation between REM% and procedural learning (c0113). Meanwhile, recent older-adult studies point to N2/N3 fast spindles instead (c0035, c0108). No study in this set manipulates REM in older adults to test whether it is causally necessary for procedural consolidation as distinct from NREM spindles.
